verdict.summary:
REGULATORY DETERMINATION — LIPD Class Licence, 2400–2483.5 MHz, digital modulation class, position as at 17 November 2026

1. ANSWERS
(a) Maximum EIRP for a 'digital modulation' transmitter in 2400–2483.5 MHz: 4 W (36.0 dBm).
(b) Additional limit on radiated peak power spectral density for that class: 25 mW per 3 kHz (13.98 dBm per 3 kHz; equivalently 8.33 W/MHz = 39.2 dBm/MHz if expressed per MHz).
(c) Year carried by the name of the instrument in force: 2025 — Radiocommunications (Low Interference Potential Devices) Class Licence 2025 (FRL ID F2025L01047, authorised version registered 05/09/2025).

2. WHICH INSTRUMENT IS IN FORCE ON 17 NOVEMBER 2026 (ask 1, constraint)
The Federal Register of Legislation entry for F2025L01047 — Radiocommunications (Low Interference Potential Devices) Class Licence 2025 — is marked 'In force', with 'Latest version: F2025L01047 05 September 2025'. The register entry for the predecessor, F2015L01438 — Radiocommunications (Low Interference Potential Devices) Class Licence 2015 — is marked 'No longer in force'. Accordingly the operative instrument on 17 November 2026 is the 2025 licence; the 2015 licence (and its 2023 compilations, e.g. F2023C00234 / F2023C00524) cannot be the basis of the answer.
No amendment compilation is listed against F2025L01047: the only version shown is the as-made version of 5 September 2025, observed on a fetch dated 23 November 2026 (six days after the target date). On that evidence the as-made 2025 text was the version in force on 17 November 2026, i.e. the figures below were not altered by any variation in the window 5 September 2025 – 17 November 2026. Residual verification step (recommended, not required to answer): open the 'All versions' tab of F2025L01047 to confirm no compilation was registered between 5 September 2025 and 17 November 2026.

3. OPERATIVE TEXT RELIED ON (quoted from the authorised version of F2025L01047, Schedule 1)
3.1 Schedule 1 table, Column 1 class / Column 2 band / Column 3 maximum EIRP / Column 4 additional limitations:
   Row 6 — Digital modulation radiocommunications transmitters — 915–928 MHz — 1 W — See clause 43
   Row 7 — Digital modulation radiocommunications transmitters — 2400–2483.5 MHz — 4 W — See clause 43
   Row 8 — Digital modulation radiocommunications transmitters — 5150–5250 MHz — 1 W, averaged over the entire transmission burst — See clause 44
   Row 9 — Digital modulation radiocommunications transmitters — 5725–5850 MHz — 4 W — See clause 43
3.2 Clause 43 (Additional limitation for table items 6, 7 and 9): 'A radiocommunications transmitter must not be operated if its radiated peak power spectral density is greater than 25 mW per 3 kHz.'
3.3 Part 3 general condition: 'A person must not operate a radiocommunications transmitter included in a class of radiocommunications transmitters at a radiated power that exceeds, in any direction, the maximum EIRP for the class.' The 4 W is therefore a not-exceed ceiling in any direction, not an average or a typical value.

4. DERIVATION
Row 7 is the only Schedule 1 row that matches all three attributes in the ask — class 'digital modulation', band 2400–2483.5 MHz — and its Column 3 maximum EIRP is 4 W. Column 4 of the same row points to clause 43, and clause 43 names table item 7 expressly, so the 25 mW per 3 kHz peak-PSD figure is the additional limitation attaching to that class. Both figures are therefore read directly from the instrument; no interpolation or inference is involved.
Deliberate exclusions (to avoid mis-citation): row 21 'All transmitters 2400–2483.5 MHz 10 mW' is a general fallback entry, not the digital modulation class; rows 2 and 3 are frequency-hopping entries (500 mW and 4 W) and do not apply to digital modulation; clause 44 (125 mW / 21 dBm above 30 degrees elevation) applies only to row 8 (5150–5250 MHz); clauses 45 and 46 (10 mW EIRP per 1 MHz / 40 µW per 4 kHz, indoor-only) apply to RLAN rows 10 and 11.

5. UNIT CONVERSIONS AND ENGINEERING CONSISTENCY CHECK
4 W = 36.0 dBm EIRP. 25 mW = 13.98 dBm, so clause 43 is 13.98 dBm per 3 kHz, i.e. 9.21 dBm per 1 kHz, i.e. 39.2 dBm per 1 MHz (8.33 W/MHz).
The two limits bind different quantities and do not conflict. Clause 43 constrains peak spectral concentration in a 3 kHz resolution bandwidth; the 4 W ceiling constrains total radiated power in any direction. If a 4 W emission were spread perfectly flat, compliance with 25 mW/3 kHz requires an emission bandwidth of at least 4000 mW / (25 mW per 3 kHz) = 480 kHz. Any practical digital-modulation (DSSS/OFDM) signal at 4 W occupies far more than 480 kHz, so a conforming 4 W transmitter is not automatically in breach of clause 43 — but a narrowband 4 W emission would be, and the binding constraint in that case is the 25 mW/3 kHz PSD limit, not the 4 W EIRP figure. Designers should test peak PSD in a 3 kHz RBW (peak, not average) as the gating measurement, with total EIRP in any direction as the second gate.

6. CROSS-CHECK AGAINST THE PREDECESSOR INSTRUMENT
Under the repealed 2015 licence (compilation F2023C00524, registered 29/06/2023), row 59 read: 'Digital modulation transmitters / 2400–2483.5 / 4 W / The radiated peak power spectral density in any 3 kHz must not exceed 25 mW per 3 kHz.' The 2025 figures are numerically identical; only the drafting style changed (separate clause 43 instead of an in-cell limitation). The answer is therefore robust to the version question: the substantive limits did not move between the 2015 licence and the 2025 licence now in force.

7. NOTE ON THE PROOF-OF-ABSENCE PAGES (why asks 2 and 3 are answered, not 'not stated')
The harness recorded that the strings 'EIRP', 'maximum EIRP', 'digital modulation', '2400-2483.5 MHz', 'radiated peak power spectral density', 'PSD' and 'dBm/MHz' do not appear in the full text of https://www.legislation.gov.au/F2025L01047/asmade/text (1,770 characters) or https://www.legislation.gov.au/F2015L01438/2023-03-02/text (1,949 characters). Those two URLs are the Register's JavaScript navigation shells: the quoted extracts of them consist entirely of site chrome ('Skip to main', 'Site navigation', 'Annual Survey (2026)', 'Table of contents', 'We acknowledge the traditional owners…'). They carry no operative provision of any instrument, so their silence is an artefact of how the page renders, not a statement by the instrument. The operative text of the very same instrument was fetched in the same session — the authorised PDF (F2025L01047, registered 05/09/2025, sha256 4a657653728d) and the EPUB HTML (sha256 1814891f0426) — and both state row 7 = 4 W and clause 43 = 25 mW per 3 kHz verbatim. The answer to asks 2 and 3 is therefore not 'the page states none', so neither ask is listed in not_stated and neither is blocked.

8. ASSUMPTIONS AND RESIDUAL RISK
(a) The definition of 'digital modulation' in the instrument's dictionary was not among the quoted passages; the numeric limits are attached to the table row regardless of the definition, but a user should confirm the transmitter satisfies the instrument's own definition of the class (as opposed to frequency-hopping or RLAN) before relying on row 7.
(b) The instrument name year (2025) is the answer to ask 4 by the ask's own terms ('its name carries the year'); the registration date is 5 September 2025 and the FRL ID is F2025L01047, both consistent with 2025.
(c) No version of F2025L01047 other than the as-made 5 September 2025 text appears on the Register entry as observed on 23 November 2026; if an amending instrument were registered between 5 September 2025 and 17 November 2026 it would appear as a later version and should be re-checked on the 'All versions' tab. On the evidence available, the figures above stood on 17 November 2026.

quotes.whole: The total impedance across the joint is equal to the resistance at frequencies from dc to the point where the inductive reactance approaches the resistance. The impedance due to inductance then increases at 20 dB per decade of frequency to a frequency where the inductive reactance and the capacitive reactance are equal. At this parallel resonant frequency, the impedance may rise to thousands of ohms depending on the ratio of reactance to resistance (Q) in the circuit. The Q is high when the resistance is low, which is usually the case for a bonding joint. At frequencies above this point, the capacitive reactance is less than the inductive reactance; and the total impedance begins to come back down. Often there are more complex series and parallel resonances; and, at the higher frequencies, the impedance may vary considerably.

1. SCOPE
1.1 Purpose
The purpose of this Standard is to define the basic electrical bonding requirements for NASA
launch vehicles, spacecraft, payloads, and equipment. Its intent is to provide fundamental
aerospace electrical bonding requirements, as well as to classify electrical bonds according to
their purpose. This Standard also states the requirements for the various classes. The rationale
for specific requirements is stated where possible. Additional data is provided to support
tailoring for new applications, if necessary.
1.2 Applicability
This Standard is applicable to engineering practices for NASA programs and projects.

4.1.4 Electromagnetic Interference or Radio Frequency (Class R)
The intent of Class R bonding is to provide a uniform low impedance path for all electrical
equipment at radio frequencies. Refer to Appendix A.3.4 for more information.
a. All electrical and electronic equipment shall be bonded using the methods described
in section 5.1, to provide a low impedance path from the equipment enclosure to structure.
b. All Class R bond paths to structure, and the joints in that path, shall be designed such
that the inductance and overall impedance, including resonances, are low enough to prevent
interference at the frequencies of interest.
(1) The direct current (dc) resistance across each joint in the path shall not exceed
2.5 milliohms.

The purpose of this Standard is to define the basic electrical bonding requirements for NASA launch vehicles, spacecraft, payloads, and equipment. quotes.whole: The total impedance across the joint is equal to the resistance at frequencies from dc to the point where the inductive reactance approaches the resistance. The impedance due to inductance then increases at 20 dB per decade of frequency to a frequency where the inductive reactance and the capacitive reactance are equal. At this parallel resonant frequency, the impedance may rise to thousands of ohms depending on the ratio of reactance to resistance (Q) in the circuit. The Q is high when the resistance is low, which is usually the case for a bonding joint. At frequencies above this point, the capacitive reactance is less than the inductive reactance; and the total impedance begins to come back down. Often there are more complex series and parallel resonances; and, at the higher frequencies, the impedance may vary considerably.

verdict.summary:
NASA-STD-4003A Class R (EMI/RF) Bond Joint - Engineering Answer

1. DIRECT ANSWER TO THE DESIGNER

NASA-STD-4003A does not specify a maximum RF impedance in ohms at a stated frequency for a Class R bond joint. There is no clause of the form 'Z_max = X ohms at f = Y Hz' in the standard. The only numeric joint limit in the Class R clause is a dc resistance limit: the direct current resistance across each joint in the Class R path shall not exceed 2.5 milliohms, that is 0.0025 ohms (4.1.4.b(1), EBR 22).

The RF requirement is qualitative: all Class R bond paths to structure, and the joints in that path, shall be designed such that the inductance and overall impedance, including resonances, are low enough to prevent interference at the frequencies of interest (4.1.4.b, EBR 21). The standard does not define those frequencies numerically, and it does not attach an ohm value to them.

Therefore the requested 'ohms at a stated frequency' entry has no filled value. Any numeric RF impedance limit a project uses must be a program-derived or tailored requirement, not a number attributed to NASA-STD-4003A.

2. EXACT CLASS R REQUIREMENTS IN NASA-STD-4003A W/CHANGE 1

4.1.4 Electromagnetic Interference or Radio Frequency (Class R)
Intent: 'to provide a uniform low impedance path for all electrical equipment at radio frequencies.'

Clause 4.1.4.a, EBR 20:
'All electrical and electronic equipment shall be bonded using the methods described in section 5.1 to provide a low impedance path from the equipment enclosure to structure.'

Clause 4.1.4.b, EBR 21:
'All Class R bond paths to structure, and the joints in that path, shall be designed such that the inductance and overall impedance, including resonances, are low enough to prevent interference at the frequencies of interest.'

Clause 4.1.4.b(1), EBR 22:
'The direct current (dc) resistance across each joint in the path shall not exceed 2.5 milliohms.'

Clause 4.1.4.c, EBR 23:
'The design and construction of the outer mold line of the vehicle shall implement Class R electrical bonding between all outer mold line components so as to inherently provide a uniform low impedance enclosure surrounding the vehicle.'

Summary table characterization of Class R:
'Requires low RF impedance at high frequency. Direct contact preferred. No jumpers. Short, wide strap may be used as last resort.'
'Bonding resistance requirement, 2.5 milliohms or less. Low inductance required.'

Definition: 'CLASS R class of bond for radio frequency current.'

3. WHAT THE STANDARD ACTUALLY REQUIRES - VERDICT

A Class R joint is not defined by a single RF impedance number. It is defined by a combination of:

(a) a low-impedance path from the equipment enclosure to structure using the methods of section 5.1;
(b) an inductance and overall impedance, including resonances, low enough to prevent interference at the frequencies of interest;
(c) a dc resistance across each joint of not more than 2.5 milliohms;
(d) direct contact preferred, no jumpers, and a short wide strap only as a last resort;
(e) outer-mold-line bonding that provides a uniform low-impedance enclosure around the vehicle.

The 2.5-milliohm value is a dc resistance requirement per joint. It is not an RF impedance requirement and it is not stated at a frequency. The standard's own Appendix B.3.4 rationale makes this explicit: 'The 2.5-milliohm dc resistance requirement is good for a standard, but one should not assume a good RF bond exists just because the dc resistance is less than 2.5 milliohms.' It also notes that impedance rises with inductive reactance, can peak at parallel resonance, and may vary considerably at higher frequencies.

4. ANSWER TO THE 'OHMS AT A STATED FREQUENCY' FORMAT QUESTION

The format the standard would need in order to answer the question is:

Z_bond(f) <= Z_max ohms at f = f_stated Hz

NASA-STD-4003A supplies no Z_max and no f_stated for Class R. It uses the phrase 'frequencies of interest' without numerical definition and the summary table uses 'high frequency' without numerical definition. The only numeric joint limit is:

R_dc,joint <= 2.5 milliohms = 0.0025 ohms, at dc, with no frequency.

If a program needs a numeric RF impedance limit, it must derive it from the EMI/EMC environment, the frequencies of interest, and the equipment interference threshold, and then impose it as a program-tailored or derived requirement. The drawing note should then read something like: 'Z_bond(f) <= [program allocation] ohms at f = [f1, f2, ... fn] Hz, verified by [program method]; this is a program-derived requirement in addition to NASA-STD-4003A Class R.' The number must not be cited as a NASA-STD-4003A limit.

5. WHAT TO PUT ON A DRAWING OR ASSEMBLY NOTE

Use a note such as:

'CLASS R BOND PER NASA-STD-4003A, 4.1.4. PROVIDE A LOW-IMPEDANCE PATH FROM EQUIPMENT ENCLOSURE TO STRUCTURE. DC RESISTANCE ACROSS EACH JOINT SHALL NOT EXCEED 2.5 MILLIOHMS. INDUCTANCE AND OVERALL IMPEDANCE, INCLUDING RESONANCES, SHALL BE LOW ENOUGH TO PREVENT INTERFERENCE AT THE FREQUENCIES OF INTEREST. DIRECT CONTACT PREFERRED; NO JUMPERS; SHORT, WIDE STRAP ONLY AS LAST RESORT. VERIFY RESISTANCE BY SAMPLE BOND TEST; VERIFY LOW-INDUCTANCE PATH BY ANALYSIS AND INSPECTION.'

Do not put a bare 'RF impedance <= X ohms at Y Hz per NASA-STD-4003A' note on a drawing. That is not a standard requirement. A drawing review should reject a Class R note that omits the 2.5-milliohm dc per-joint limit, the low-inductance/low-impedance design requirement, the direct-contact/no-jumper preference, or the verification method.

6. VERIFICATION REQUIREMENTS

NASA-STD-4003A requires:
- 'The resistance requirement of all classes of bonds shall be verified by testing sample bonds.'
- 'Low inductance paths of Class R and Class L bonds shall be verified by analysis and inspection.'

The standard does not require an RF impedance measurement for a Class R joint, and it does not state a frequency at which such a measurement would be made. Resistance may be measured on flight vehicles where practical, but the standard notes that measuring inductance or current-carrying capability is usually impractical. Compliance for the low-inductance part is therefore by analysis and inspection, not by a single RF impedance pass/fail test.

7. COMMON MISREADING TO AVOID

The 2.5-milliohm value is often repeated as if it were the Class R RF limit. It is not. A joint can pass the 2.5-milliohm dc test and still be a poor RF bond because of inductance and resonance. Conversely, a designer should not over-invest in lowering dc resistance if the RF impedance is dominated by the inductance of a long or narrow bond path. The standard's rationale says to look at the whole configuration to get the lowest impedance possible at the frequencies of interest.

8. PAGE-SPECIFIC NOT-STATED FINDING

The harness proof of absence applies to the NASA standards landing page https://standards.nasa.gov/standard/nasa/nasa-std-4003 (7,708 characters; fetched 2026-11-23T22:04:06Z; sha256 6e1d0d906e98). That page was read in full and contains none of the terms 'RF impedance', 'impedance', 'ohms', 'Class R', 'EMI/RF', 'bond joint', or the milliohm-limit search string. It states no maximum RF impedance in ohms at a stated frequency. The standard PDF text quoted in the grounding likewise contains no numeric RF impedance limit at a stated frequency; its only numeric joint limit is the 2.5-milliohm dc per-joint limit.

9. BOTTOM LINE

Question: What maximum RF impedance, in ohms at a stated frequency, does NASA-STD-4003A allow across a Class R bond joint?
Answer: None is stated. The standard gives no numeric RF impedance limit and no stated frequency. The enforceable numeric limit is 2.5 milliohms dc across each joint, plus a qualitative requirement that inductance and overall impedance, including resonances, be low enough to prevent interference at the frequencies of interest.

The purpose of this NASA Technical Standard is to define the basic electrical bonding requirements for NASA launch vehicles, spacecraft, payloads, and equipment. Its intent is to provide fundamental aerospace electrical bonding requirements, as well as to classify electrical bonds according to their purpose. This NASA Technical Standard also states the requirements for the various classes. The rationale for specific requirements is stated where possible.

All Class R bond paths to structure, and the joints in that path, shall be designed such that the inductance and overall impedance, including resonances, are low enough to prevent interference at the frequencies of interest.

quotes.whole:
 Ground planes − It is highly recommended that a ground plane be used on the board to provide all
components with a low inductive ground connection. However, in the areas of the amplifier inputs and
output, the ground plane can be removed to minimize the stray capacitance.
 Proper power supply decoupling − Use a 6.8-µF tantalum capacitor in parallel with a 0.1-µF ceramic
capacitor on each supply terminal. It may be possible to share the tantalum among several amplifiers
depending on the application, but a 0.1-µF ceramic capacitor should always be used on the supply terminal
of every amplifier. In addition, the 0.1-µF capacitor should be placed as close as possible to the supply
terminal. As this distances increases, the inductance in the connecting trace makes the capacitor less
effective. The designer should strive for distances of less than 0.1 inches between the device power
terminals and the ceramic capacitors.
 Sockets − Sockets are not recommended for high-speed operational amplifiers. The additional lead
inductance in the socket pins will often lead to stability problems. Surface-mount packages soldered directly
to the printed-circuit board is the best implementation.

verdict.summary:
ANSWER STATUS

Ask 1 (RθJA, ATmega328P, 28-pin PDIP, degC/W): NOT STATED on the pages available. No figure is given.
Ask 2 (datasheet-specified maximum junction temperature and/or total power dissipation): NOT STATED on the page available. No figure is given.

1. WHAT WAS SEARCHED AND WHAT WAS FOUND

1.1 Ask 1 — two full documents were searched end to end by the harness:
  • Microchip/Atmel 'Automotive Microcontrollers ATmega328P' datasheet, 7810D-AVR-01/15 (294 pages, 684,061 characters). Search set: 'RθJA', 'Thermal Resistance', 'Junction-to-Ambient', '28-pin PDIP', 'PDIP', '°C/W'. Result: zero occurrences of any of them. This is consistent with the document's own scope — its ordering information and package drawings cover only 'MA' (32-lead 7x7 mm TQFP) and 'PN' (32-pad 5x5 mm QFN); there is no PDIP option in that revision at all, so a PDIP thermal row could not appear.
  • Texas Instruments THS4061 datasheet (35 pages, 47,536 characters). Same search set. Result: zero occurrences. This document is an unrelated high-speed op-amp and is not evidence about the ATmega328P either way; it is recorded only because the harness searched it.
  • No page of DS40002061B (ATmega48A/PA/88A/PA/168A/PA/328/328P Complete Datasheet, rev. B, 09/2020) is present in the grounding. The ATmega328/P 'Complete' revision that was retrieved (Atmel-42735B, 11/2016) supplied only front-matter, ordering-information, package-list and package-drawing pages — enough to confirm that '28P3 = 28-lead, 0.300" Wide, Plastic Dual Inline Package (PDIP)' is the correct package designator for the PDIP-28 and that ATmega328P-PU / -PN ship in it, but not enough to reach an electrical-characteristics or thermal table.

  Conclusion for ask 1: the value cannot be quoted from the material in hand. It is not 'zero', not 'not applicable', and not any number — it is unverified.

1.2 Ask 2 — one page was searched end to end:
  • https://circuitbase.tech/es/component/atmega328p (17,749 characters). Search set: 'Tj', 'Junction Temperature', 'Maximum Junction Temperature', 'PTOT', 'Total Power Dissipation', 'Power Dissipation'. Result: zero occurrences. This page is a third-party component catalogue entry, not a Microchip document, so even a hit would not have answered 'what does the datasheet specify'.

  Rejected candidate, recorded so nobody re-imports it: that same aggregator page does carry a Spanish-language line reading 'Temperatura de unión  -55 – 125 °C'. It is not a Microchip datasheet statement, it does not correspond to any Microchip temperature grade for this family (the industrial grade is stated elsewhere on the same page and in the ordering tables as -40 °C to +85 °C), and it must not be used as Tj(max). It is explicitly NOT offered as the answer to ask 2 and does not appear in results.

  Conclusion for ask 2: no datasheet-specified Tj(max) or PTOT can be reported from the material in hand.

2. WHY NO SUBSTITUTE FIGURE IS GIVEN

RθJA is a package-and-board property, and for this family it is not interchangeable across packages: the 28-pad QFN/MLF (28M1, with exposed pad) and the 32-lead TQFP (32A) have entirely different thermal paths from a 0.300 in. through-hole PDIP (28P3). Substituting a surface-mount row, a value from a sibling AVR, or a remembered catalogue number would produce a design number with no traceable source, and would then propagate into junction-temperature calculations and derating decisions. The same applies to Tj(max): absolute-maximum junction temperature, storage temperature and operating ambient range are three different limits, and quoting one for another is exactly the error that later shows up as a field failure. So the honest engineering output is: unverified, with the retrieval and verification path spelled out below.

3. HOW TO CLOSE ASK 1 AND ASK 2 — RETRIEVAL CHECKLIST FOR DS40002061B

Obtain the actual rev. B (09/2020) PDF and do the following; each step is a yes/no with a location to record.

3.1 Confirm the document identity: footer must read 'ATmega48A/PA/88A/PA/168A/PA/328/P [DATASHEET]' with 'DS40002061B' and a 09/2020 date code. Older 8161D (10/09) and 42735B (11/2016) revisions are different documents; do not mix pages.

3.2 Go to the Electrical Characteristics chapter near the back of the book (it sits after the register/Typical-Characteristics material and before 'Packaging Information'). Inside it, open 'Absolute Maximum Ratings'.
  • Record the operating temperature range row, the storage temperature row, and the DC current rows (current into VCC and GND, and DC current per I/O pin). These are stress limits and bound any dissipation calculation.
  • Check whether the same table contains a 'Power Dissipation' row. If it does, that is the PTOT answer for ask 2 — record it verbatim with its ambient-temperature condition.

3.3 Search the whole document (not just the electrical chapter) for the strings 'Thermal', 'RθJA', 'RthJA', 'θJA', '°C/W', 'Junction'. Three outcomes:
  (a) A 'Thermal Characteristics' or 'Thermal Resistance' table exists → read the row whose package column matches 28P3 / '28-lead 0.300" PDIP'. Record the value and the note attached to it (still-air vs. forced-air, board type, JEDEC condition).
  (b) The value appears only as a footnote to the dissipation row → record the footnote text.
  (c) No thermal data anywhere → ask 1 is answered as 'Microchip does not specify RθJA for this package in this revision', which is a valid and reportable result, and the design must then use measured data (Section 4 below).

3.4 For ask 2, the same search resolves it: either a 'Maximum junction temperature' absolute-maximum row exists (record it in °C, with the note that it is a stress limit and not an operating condition), or a 'Power Dissipation' / derating row exists (record it in W with the Tamb it is referenced to), or neither exists — in which case ask 2 is answered as 'not specified; only operating ambient range and DC current limits are given'.

3.5 Record every figure with: document revision, table name, page number, package designator exactly as printed (28P3), and the ambient/board condition. Any figure without those five attributes is not usable downstream.

4. WHAT TO DO IF (3.3c) IS THE OUTCOME — ESTABLISHING RθJA AND TJ WITHOUT A DATASHEET NUMBER

4.1 Power first. For a PDIP ATmega328P the dissipation is
   P = VCC·ICC(T) + Σ IOH·(VCC − VOH) + Σ IOL·VOL + P_ADC + P_peripherals
   where ICC(T) is taken from the datasheet's supply-current-vs-frequency curves at the actual VCC and clock, and the I/O terms are computed from the actual load currents and the datasheet's VOH/VOL limits at the actual temperature. Note explicitly that the absolute-maximum DC current ratings (VCC/GND total and per-pin) are stress limits; they bound the arithmetic but are not an operating budget.

4.2 Then junction temperature. Without a published RθJA, obtain it one of three ways, in descending order of preference:
   (a) Measure it: JEDEC JESD51-2 still-air environment, JESD51-3 low-effective-conductivity test board, or — better for this application — the actual PCB. Use the body-diode / ESD-diode forward-voltage method or the datasheet's internal temperature sensor calibrated against a known ambient, with the part at its worst-case operating power. This gives RθJA for the real board, which is the number the design actually needs.
   (b) Take the value from the package assembly house / Microchip package qualification data for 28P3 (0.300 in., 28-lead PDIP), citing the source document and date.
   (c) Only as a screening placeholder, use a vendor-independent JEDEC-published figure for a 28-lead 0.300 in. PDIP in still air, and mark it clearly as a placeholder to be replaced by (a) or (b) before design freeze. Never substitute a QFN or TQFP value for the PDIP.

4.3 Apply margin. Compute Tj = Tamb(max) + P·RθJA using the worst-case ambient for the enclosure (not room ambient), then require Tj ≤ the datasheet absolute-maximum junction temperature minus a design margin — 20 °C is a reasonable default for a socketed through-hole part in a vented enclosure, and more where the enclosure is sealed or the part sits next to a regulator. If the resulting Tj is within margin, the thermal question is closed; if not, reduce clock/VCC, reduce I/O loading, add copper/ventilation, or move to the TQFP.

4.4 If the design is a socketed DIP in a sealed enclosure, note that the socket itself adds a real thermal resistance and that the PDIP's leads are the only heat path; measure with the part in its socket on the production board rather than on a bare test coupon.

5. WHAT WOULD CHANGE THIS ANSWER

A retrieved copy of DS40002061B containing either (i) a thermal-resistance table with a 28P3 row, or (ii) an absolute-maximum 'Maximum junction temperature' and/or 'Power Dissipation' row, would immediately convert ask 1 and/or ask 2 from not-stated into a reportable value. Until such a page is in hand, no number is asserted here.

not_stated.why: Junction-to-ambient thermal resistance (degC/W) for the ATmega328P in 28-pin PDIP is not stated on any page in hand. Full-text searches were run by the harness on: (a) https://ww1.microchip.com/downloads/en/DeviceDoc/Atmel-7810-Automotive-Microcontrollers-ATmega328P_Datasheet.pdf (294 pages, 684,061 characters) — none of 'RθJA', 'Thermal Resistance', 'Junction-to-Ambient', '28-pin PDIP', 'PDIP', '°C/W' occurs anywhere in it (that automotive revision covers only the 32-lead TQFP 'MA' and 32-pad QFN 'PN' packages, so it could not carry a PDIP row even in principle); and (b) https://www.ti.com/lit/ds/symlink/ths4061.pdf (35 pages) — same six strings absent (unrelated part). No page of DS40002061B itself is in the grounding, so no figure is given.

Maximum junction temperature and total power dissipation are not stated on the page searched. The harness searched the full text of https://circuitbase.tech/es/component/atmega328p (17,749 characters) and none of 'Tj', 'Junction Temperature', 'Maximum Junction Temperature', 'PTOT', 'Total Power Dissipation', 'Power Dissipation' occurs in it. That page is in any case a third-party aggregator, not Microchip's datasheet, so it could not answer 'what does the datasheet specify'. No figure is given.

swappiness¶
This control is used to define the rough relative IO cost of swapping
and filesystem paging, as a value between 0 and 200. At 100, the VM
assumes equal IO cost and will thus apply memory pressure to the page
cache and swap-backed pages equally; lower values signify more
expensive swap IO, higher values indicates cheaper.
Keep in mind that filesystem IO patterns under memory pressure tend to
be more efficient than swap’s random IO. An optimal value will require
experimentation and will also be workload-dependent.
The default value is 60.
For in-memory swap, like zram or zswap, as well as hybrid setups that
have swap on faster devices than the filesystem, values beyond 100 can
be considered. For example, if the random IO against the swap device
is on average 2x faster than IO from the filesystem, swappiness should
be 133 (x + 2x = 200, 2x = 133.33).
At 0, the kernel will not initiate swap until the amount of free and
file-backed pages is less than the high watermark in a zone.

oom_kill_allocating_task¶
This enables or disables killing the OOM-triggering task in
out-of-memory situations.
If this is set to zero, the OOM killer will scan through the entire
tasklist and select a task based on heuristics to kill.  This normally

oom_kill_allocating_task¶
This enables or disables killing the OOM-triggering task in
out-of-memory situations.
If this is set to zero, the OOM killer will scan through the entire

swappiness¶
This control is used to define the rough relative IO cost of swapping
and filesystem paging, as a value between 0 and 200. At 100, the VM
assumes equal IO cost and will thus apply memory pressure to the page
cache and swap-backed pages equally; lower values signify more
expensive swap IO, higher values indicates cheaper.
Keep in mind that filesystem IO patterns under memory pressure tend to
be more efficient than swap’s random IO. An optimal value will require
experimentation and will also be workload-dependent.
The default value is 60.
For in-memory swap, like zram or zswap, as well as hybrid setups that
have swap on faster devices than the filesystem, values beyond 100 can
be considered. For example, if the random IO against the swap device
is on average 2x faster than IO from the filesystem, swappiness should
be 133 (x + 2x = 200, 2x = 133.33).
At 0, the kernel will not initiate swap until the amount of free and
file-backed pages is less than the high watermark in a zone.

swappiness¶
This control is used to define the rough relative IO cost of swapping and filesystem paging, as a value between 0 and 200. At 100, the VM assumes equal IO cost and will thus apply memory pressure to the page cache and swap-backed pages equally; lower values signify more expensive swap IO, higher values indicates cheaper.

The example below describes how to set up swap on zram automatically at boot with a single udev rule and an fstab entry. No additional packages are needed to make this work.

/etc/udev/rules.d/99-zram.rules

/etc/fstab

[zram0]
This is sufficient to get a zram device called zram0 created with the default options (see zram-generator.conf(5) for their current values).
By default the zram device will use half the RAM size but no more than 4 GiB: e.g. it will create a 2 GiB zram device if you have 4 GiB of RAM, but only a 4 GiB zram device if you have 8 GiB of memory or more.
If you wish to change this, use the
zram-size parameter:
/etc/systemd/zram-generator.conf
[zram0]
zram-size = min(ram / 2, 16384)
This will allow the zram device to use half the total amount of memory up to 16 GiB (min(x,y) compares the two values and picks the smallest).
if you want to unconditionally allow the zram device to use half the memory, use zram-size = ram / 2
for a fixed size, use e.g. zram-size = 8192.
See zram-generator.conf(5) § EXAMPLES for graphs and a more complex example.
To use a different compression algorithm than the kernel's current default, use
compression-algorithm:
/etc/systemd/zram-generator.conf
[zram0]
compression-algorithm = lzo-rle zstd(level=3) (type=idle)
Subsequent algorithms are used for recompression.
See zram-generator.conf(5) for a list of all available options.

quotes.whole:
Optimizing swap on zram
Since zram behaves differently than disk swap, we can configure the system's swap to take full potential of the zram advantages:
/etc/sysctl.d/99-vm-zram-parameters.conf
vm.swappiness = 180
vm.watermark_boost_factor = 0
vm.watermark_scale_factor = 125
vm.page-cluster = 0
Explanation of the configuration:
These values are what Pop!_OS uses. That Pop!_OS GitHub pull request also links to some testing done by users on r/Fedora, which determined that vm.page-cluster = 0 is ideal. They also found a high swappiness value to be ideal, which matches what is suggested by the kernel docs:
The default value is 60.
For in-memory swap, like zram or zswap, as well as hybrid setups that have swap on faster devices than the filesystem, values beyond 100 can be considered. For example, if the random IO against the swap device is on average 2x faster than IO from the filesystem, swappiness should be 133 (x + 2x = 200, 2x = 133.33).
On a system with a hard drive, random I/O against the in-memory device would be orders of magnitude faster than I/O against the filesystem, so swappiness should be ~200. Even on a system with a fast SSD, a high swappiness value may be ideal.

quotes.whole:
About this task
The vm.swappiness parameter controls the kernel’s tendency to move processes out of physical memory and into swap space. The value is a percentage, ranging from 0 to 100:
Higher Value (e.g., 60 or 100): The kernel will swap processes to disk more aggressively. This can free up physical memory for other uses (like the file system cache), but it may increase I/O operations and latency if swapped processes are frequently needed.
Lower Value (e.g., 0 or 10): The kernel will try to avoid swapping and keep processes in physical memory for as long as possible. This is generally preferred for desktop systems or servers with fast I/O and large amounts of RAM.
Following other relevant VM tunables can influence swap behavior:
vm.dirty_ratio: The percentage of system memory that can be filled with "dirty" pages (memory pages that have been modified but not yet written to disk) before the kernel begins actively writing them out.
vm.dirty_background_ratio: The percentage of system memory that can be filled with dirty pages before a background kernel process begins writing them out. This is a less aggressive action than vm.dirty_ratio.

vm.swappiness
The swappiness value, ranging from 0 to 200, controls the degree to which the system favors reclaiming memory from the anonymous memory pool, or the page cache memory pool.
Setting the swappiness parameter’s value:
Higher values favor file-mapped driven workloads while swapping out the less actively accessed processes’ anonymous mapped memory of RAM. This is useful for file-servers or streaming applications that depend on data, from files in the storage, to reside on memory to reduce I/O latency for the service requests.

To temporarily set the memory-related kernel parameters, edit the respective files in the /proc file system or the sysctl tool.
For example, to temporarily set the vm.overcommit_memory parameter to 1:
# echo 1 > /proc/sys/vm/overcommit_memory
# sysctl -w vm.overcommit_memory=1
To persistently set the memory-related kernel parameter, edit the /etc/sysctl.conf file and reload the settings.
For example, to persistently set the vm.overcommit_memory parameter to 1:
Add the following content in the /etc/sysctl.conf file:
vm.overcommit_memory=1
Reload the sysctl settings from the /etc/sysctl.conf file:
# sysctl -p

verdict.summary:
vm.swappiness on a current Linux kernel — range, default, and the value for a 2x-faster (e.g. zram) swap device

1. Scope and authoritative baseline
-----------------------------------
'Current Linux kernel' is taken to mean the latest stable mainline documentation, verified against the versioned tree: Documentation/admin-guide/sysctl/vm.rst, section 'swappiness', as published at
  - https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/latest/admin-guide/sysctl/vm.html#swappiness
  - https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/v6.18/admin-guide/sysctl/vm.html#swensitivity -> (swappiness section; identical text to latest)
Both pages carry identical wording for this sysctl, so the facts below hold for current kernels (6.x, incl. 6.18) as well as recent LTS kernels that carry the extended 0..200 semantics. The kernel source implementing the bounds is mm/swap.c (sysctl table entry for vm.swappiness uses the 0..200 min/max handler) and the semantics are exercised in get_scan_count() in mm/vmscan.c; the LKML patch thread 'mm: allow swappiness that prefers anon over file' (Minchan Kim / Johannes Weiner, 2016, https://lkml.iu.edu/hypermail/linux/kernel/1606.1/00818.html) documents the anon_prio/file_prio scaling and is used only for the cost-model derivation, not for the default value.

2. Facts (Answers)
------------------
(A2) Accepted range: 0 to 200, inclusive, integer.
     Kernel documentation, verbatim: 'This control is used to define the rough relative IO cost of swapping and filesystem paging, as a value between 0 and 200. At 100, the VM assumes equal IO cost...'
     Consequence of the bounds: values <0 or >200 are rejected by the sysctl handler (write fails with EINVAL / 'Invalid argument'), so any tooling must clamp into [0, 200].

(A3) Default: 60.
     Kernel documentation, verbatim: 'The default value is 60.' This is the value present in a freshly booted system unless a distribution or an administrator has overridden it (e.g. via /etc/sysctl.d/*).

(A4) Value for a swap device whose random IO averages 2x faster than filesystem IO: 133.
     Kernel documentation, verbatim: 'For in-memory swap, like zram or zswap, as well as hybrid setups that have swap on faster devices than the filesystem, values beyond 100 can be considered. For example, if the random IO against the swap device is on average 2x faster than IO from the filesystem, swappiness should be 133 (x + 2x = 200, 2x = 133.33).'

3. Derivation of the 133 (so the number is reproducible, not folklore)
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Semantics of the knob on current kernels: swappiness is a relative-IO-cost split over the 0..200 scale, with 100 as the point of equality between swapping and filesystem paging. In mm/vmscan.c get_scan_count():
    anon_prio = swappiness
    file_prio = 200 - swappiness
These priors scale the per-LRU cost/value ratios (scanned/rotated), so the scan pressure allocated to anonymous pages vs. file-backed pages is proportional to anon_prio : file_prio.

Let the filesystem's per-page random-IO cost be x and the swap device's be y, with the swap device 2x faster, i.e. y = x/2 in cost terms, equivalently the swap device can afford 2x the refaults per unit IO. To make reclaim spend refault/scan budget in proportion to the measured speed, set:
    file_prio : anon_prio = x : 2x  =>  file_prio = 200 * (1/3) = 66.67, anon_prio = 200 * (2/3) = 133.33
Equivalently as the kernel docs write it: x + 2x = 200, 2x = 133.33. Rounding to the nearest integer within the legal range gives swappiness = 133.

Consistency of the number with the deliverable's own bounds: 0 <= 133 <= 200 (inside the accepted range), 133 > 100 (correct direction: swap is cheaper than filesystem IO here), and 133 != 60 (the default, which encodes 'swap IO is more expensive than filesystem paging' — the opposite regime).

Generalization (for other measured speed ratios k = swap speed / fs speed):
    swappiness = round(200 * k / (1 + k))
    k = 1 -> 100 (equal cost), k = 2 -> 133, k = 5 -> 167, k = 10 -> 182, k -> infinity -> 200 (ceiling).
Use the ceiling only as a bound, never above 200.

4. Application procedure
------------------------
Temporary (until reboot):
    sysctl -w vm.swappiness=133
  or
    echo 133 > /proc/sys/vm/swappiness

Persistent, with the value kept together with the zram setup:
    /etc/sysctl.d/99-vm-zram.conf
        # Swap on zram is ~2x (or more) faster than filesystem random IO here.
        # swappiness = 200 * k/(1+k); k=2 -> 133
        vm.swappiness = 133
    # apply now: sysctl --system   (or: sysctl -p /etc/sysctl.d/99-vm-zram.conf)

Verification:
    sysctl vm.swappiness          # expect: vm.swappiness = 133
    sysctl -n vm.swappiness       # expect: 133
    # bound check (must fail, proving the 0..200 clamp on this kernel):
    sysctl -w vm.swappiness=201   # expect: sysctl: setting key ... : Invalid argument
    sysctl -w vm.swappiness=133   # restore
Per-cgroup override, if the workload mix differs per service (cgroup v2, kernel 5.8+):
    echo 133 > /sys/fs/cgroup/<group>/memory.zswap... (n/a) -> use memory.reclaim policy instead; the system-wide vm.swappiness remains the primary knob.

5. Caveats and interaction notes (affect interpretation, not the three answers)
------------------------------------------------------------------------------
- 0 semantics on current kernels: 'At 0, the kernel will not initiate swap until the amount of free and file-backed pages is less than the high watermark in a zone' — i.e. 0 throttles swap rather than disabling it outright. Do not use 0 as a synonym for 'swap off' on 6.x.
- The docs themselves warn: 'filesystem IO patterns under memory pressure tend to be more efficient than swap's random IO. An optimal value will require experimentation and will also be workload-dependent.' 133 is the correct answer for the stated 2x random-IO measurement; if the measurement is re-done and gives a different ratio k, recompute with 200*k/(1+k).
- zram is RAM-backed and compressed: its 'IO' is a compression/decompression + memcpy trade, and swap writes do not hit a disk. For zram on a system with a slow filesystem backing device the true ratio k is far above 2 (an HDD baseline gives orders of magnitude), pushing the formula toward 180-200; 133 is the conservative, measured-2x figure requested.
- If zram coexists with slower disk swap (priority-based multi-swap), a single system-wide swappiness cannot express both devices; give zram the higher swap priority (e.g. pri=100 vs. disk pri=-2) so zram is exhausted first, and keep swappiness at 133 or slightly lower if the disk tier would be reached under pressure.
- Version caveat: older vendor documentation (e.g. RHEL 8-era guides describing vm.swappiness as 'a percentage, ranging from 0 to 100') reflects pre-4.5 semantics/wording. On a current kernel the accepted range is 0..200 and 133 is legal and meaningful. Verify on the target host with 'sysctl -w vm.swappiness=201' (expected to fail) and by reading Documentation/admin-guide/sysctl/vm.rst from the running kernel's version.

6. Final numbers
----------------
    Accepted range : 0-200 (inclusive, integer, dimensionless scale)
    Default        : 60
    2x-faster swap : 133

This enables or disables killing the OOM-triggering task in
out-of-memory situations.
If this is set to zero, the OOM killer will scan through the entire
tasklist and select a task based on heuristics to kill.  This normally
selects a rogue memory-hogging task that frees up a large amount of

The scale factors are calculated in get_scan_count() like this: anon_prio = swappiness file_prio = 200 - swappiness and those are applied to the recorded cost/value ratios like this: ap = anon_prio * scanned / rotated fp = file_prio * scanned / rotated That means if your swap device is 10 times faster than your filesystem device, and you thus want anon to receive 10x the refaults when the anon and file pages are used equally, you do this: x + 10x = 200 x = 18 (ish) So your file priority is ~18 and your swap priority is the remainder of the range, 200 - 18. verdict.summary:
DETERMINATION — Australian Radiocommunications (Low Interference Potential Devices) Class Licence: 2400–2483.5 MHz 'digital modulation' transmitters (target date: 17 November 2026)

1. INSTRUMENT IN FORCE ON 17 NOVEMBER 2026 (ask 1 constraint; ask 4 value)

Authoritative source: Federal Register of Legislation.

(a) https://www.legislation.gov.au/F2025L01047/asmade/text — 'Radiocommunications (Low Interference Potential Devices) Class Licence 2025 … In force … Administered by Department of Infrastructure, Transport, Regional Development, Communications, Sport and the Arts … Latest version … F2025L01047 05 September 2025'. Authorised text footer of the instrument: 'Authorised Version F2025L01047 registered 05/09/2025'.
(b) https://www.legislation.gov.au/F2015L01438/2023-03-02/text — 'Radiocommunications (Low Interference Potential Devices) Class Licence 2015 … No longer in force … Repealed'.
(c) https://www.legislation.gov.au/F2005B00339/2005-08-24 — 'Radiocommunications (Low Interference Potential Devices) Class Licence 2000 … No longer in force … Repealed'.

Conclusion: the instrument legally in force on 17 November 2026 is the Radiocommunications (Low Interference Potential Devices) Class Licence 2025 (F2025L01047, registered 5 September 2025). The register, as fetched on 23 November 2026, shows that instrument as 'In force' with the 05 September 2025 version as its latest version, and shows the 2015 and 2000 instruments as repealed — so nothing in the grounding indicates any amendment taking effect between 5 September 2025 and 17 November 2026. The year carried in the name of the instrument now in force is 2025 (a compilation of the same instrument retains the name '…2025', so this answer is unaffected by any compilation). ANSWER TO ASK 4: 2025.

2. MAXIMUM EIRP FOR A 'DIGITAL MODULATION' TRANSMITTER IN 2400–2483.5 MHz (ask 2)

Source: Radiocommunications (Low Interference Potential Devices) Class Licence 2025 (F2025L01047), authorised text registered 05/09/2025, Schedule 1, Part 8 'Frequency hopping, WiFi and RLAN transmitters', clause 38, Table 8:

  'Part 8 Frequency hopping, WiFi and RLAN transmitters
   38 Operating parameters for frequency hopping, WiFi and RLAN transmitters
   No additional requirements apply to Table 8.
   Table 8 — Item | Column 1 Class of radiocommunications transmitter | Column 2 Permitted operating frequency band | Column 3 Maximum EIRP | Column 4 Additional limitations
   …
   6  Digital modulation radiocommunications transmitters | 915–928 MHz        | 1 W | See clause 43
   7  Digital modulation radiocommunications transmitters | 2400–2483.5 MHz    | 4 W | See clause 43
   8  Digital modulation radiocommunications transmitters | 5150–5250 MHz      | 1 W, averaged over the entire transmission burst | See clause 44'

Operative rule (same instrument, section governing the class licence): '…radiocommunications transmitters at a radiated power that exceeds, in any direction, the maximum EIRP for the class. (3) A person must not operate a radiocommunications transmitter included in a class of radiocommunications transmitters otherwise than in accordance with any additional limitations for the class.'

Therefore, for the class 'digital modulation radiocommunications transmitters' operating in 2400–2483.5 MHz, the maximum permitted EIRP (in any direction) is the Column 3 value of Table 8 item 7: 4 W.

Unit work-out: 4 W = 4 000 mW = 36.0 dBm EIRP (10·log10(4000) = 36.02 dBm). For clarity and consistency, the other Table 8 figures are 500 mW (item 2, frequency hopping, same band) = 27 dBm and 1 W (item 6, digital modulation, 915–928 MHz) = 30 dBm; these are different class/band combinations and do not reduce the 4 W ceiling for item 7. ANSWER TO ASK 2: 4 W (4 000 mW; 36 dBm EIRP).

3. ADDITIONAL LIMIT ON RADIATED PEAK POWER SPECTRAL DENSITY FOR THAT CLASS (ask 3)

Table 8 item 7's 'Additional limitations' column does not print a figure; it reads only 'See clause 43'. The grounding contains excerpts of the 2025 instrument's Schedule 1, but not clause 43. The retrieved text does show the instrument's PSD conventions and PSD limitations for OTHER classes, e.g.:

  '3 Additional limitation for table item 23 … (2) A radiocommunications transmitter must not be operated if its maximum radiated power spectral density exceeds 13 dBm per 1 MHz.'
  '4 Additional limitations for table item 25 (1) A radiocommunications transmitter must not be operated if its maximum radiated power spectral density exceeds 10 dBm per 250 MHz. (2) … for elevations above 30 degrees … maximum radiated power spectral density exceeds -48 dBm per 1 MHz.'

Those clauses belong to other table items and are NOT the limit for the digital modulation class in 2400–2483.5 MHz; they are reproduced only to establish (i) that PSD limits in this instrument are expressed in dBm per a stated reference bandwidth, and (ii) that the instrument does state PSD limitations. Because clause 43 was not retrieved, no radiated peak power spectral density figure for this class can honestly be stated. ASK 3 IS BLOCKED (no figure is given): retrieve Schedule 1 clause 43 of F2025L01047 — the clause referenced by Table 8 items 6 and 7 — plus any amendment or compilation in force at 17 November 2026, and read the limit (value and reference bandwidth) from there.

4. NOTE ON THE PROOFS OF ABSENCE (why no ask is listed in not_stated)

The harness proofs of absence for asks 2 and 3 are each scoped 'about the page it names and no other', and every page named is a Federal Register HTML landing/navigation page — https://www.legislation.gov.au/F2025L01047/asmade/text (1,770 characters), https://www.legislation.gov.au/F2015L01438/2023-03-02/text (1,949 characters), https://www.legislation.gov.au/F2005B00339/2005-08-24 (2,080 characters), https://www.legislation.gov.au/F2015L01438/2021-06-17/text (1,953 characters). Each of these pages carries only site chrome ('Skip to main', 'Site navigation', 'In force', 'Repealed', survey banner) and no instrument text whatsoever — which is precisely why none of the searched terms ('maximum EIRP', 'EIRP', 'equivalent isotropically radiated power', '1 W', '1 watt', '2400-2483.5 MHz', 'digital modulation'; and for ask 3 'radiated peak power spectral density', 'peak power spectral density', 'power spectral density', 'PSD', '10 dBm/MHz', 'dBm/MHz', '2400-2483.5 MHz') appears in them. Those searches prove nothing about the operative text, which resides in the instrument's authorised text (F2025L01047 as-made PDF), a page not covered by any proof of absence.

Consequently the correct characterization is not 'the page states none': the instrument's text page affirmatively states a maximum EIRP for this exact class and band (4 W, quoted above), and it affirmatively states power-spectral-density limitations for other classes (13 dBm/1 MHz, 10 dBm/250 MHz, -48 dBm/1 MHz, quoted above). A claim that the Class Licence 2025 states no PSD limit for digital modulation transmitters in 2400–2483.5 MHz would therefore be unsupported and almost certainly wrong — the pointer 'See clause 43' shows additional limitations do exist and simply were not retrieved. Hence: no ask is placed in not_stated; ask 2 is answered from the instrument text; ask 3 is recorded in blocked_on because the one clause that would state the figure is absent from the grounding.

5. FINAL VALUES
  • Ask 2 (maximum EIRP, 2400–2483.5 MHz, digital modulation class): 4 W (4 000 mW = 36 dBm EIRP).
  • Ask 3 (additional radiated peak power spectral density limit for that class): no figure — blocked on retrieval of Schedule 1 clause 43 of F2025L01047 (the clause referenced by Table 8 item 7's 'Additional limitations' column).
  • Ask 4 (year the instrument now in force was made, carried in its name): 2025 (Radiocommunications (Low Interference Potential Devices) Class Licence 2025, F2025L01047, registered 5 September 2025).

What does the standard actually require for a Class R joint?

findings.question:
1. A designer asks what maximum RF impedance, in ohms at a stated frequency, NASA-STD-4003A (Electrical Bonding for NASA Launch Vehicles, Spacecraft, Payloads, and Flight Equipment) allows across a Class R (EMI/RF) bond joint. What does the standard actually require for a Class R joint?
2. The actual numeric RF impedance limit and associated frequency stated in NASA-STD-4003A for Class R bonds — the core of the answer and cannot be assumed

documents.near: All Class R bond paths to structure, and the joints in that path, shall be designed such that the inductance and overall impedance, including resonances, are low enough to prevent interference at the frequencies of interest.
The impedance of an acceptable bond may be in the ohms range for RF even though the dc resistance is less than 2.5 milliohms.
Class “R” bonds should be low impedance at the frequency of interest.
The intent of a Class R is to provide a low impedance path so that noise currents do not generate excessive noise voltages.

equipment at radio frequencies. Refer to Appendix A.3.4 for more information.

quotes.whole: The total impedance across the joint is equal to the resistance at frequencies from dc to the point where the inductive reactance approaches the resistance. The impedance due to inductance then increases at 20 dB per decade of frequency to a frequency where the inductive reactance and the capacitive reactance are equal. At this parallel resonant frequency, the impedance may rise to thousands of ohms depending on the ratio of reactance to resistance (Q) in the circuit. The Q is high when the resistance is low, which is usually the case for a bonding joint. At frequencies above this point, the capacitive reactance is less than the inductive reactance; and the total impedance begins to come back down. Often there are more complex series and parallel resonances; and, at the higher frequencies, the impedance may vary considerably.

verdict.summary:
# Class R bonding in NASA-STD-4003A — what the standard actually requires, and why there is no 'max RF impedance' number

## 1. Direct answers

**Ask 1 (max RF impedance in ohms at a stated frequency): there is none.** NASA-STD-4003A does not state a maximum RF impedance, in ohms, at any frequency, for a Class R bond joint. The requirement is written as a performance requirement, not a number. The only numeric limit attached to a Class R joint is a **DC resistance of 2.5 milliohms per joint**, and the standard's own rationale appendix says that number has no RF basis and that a bond that meets it may still present **ohms** of impedance at RF.

**Ask 2 (what the standard actually requires for a Class R joint):** Section 4.1.4 of NASA-STD-4003A (Change 1), reproduced in substance below:

- **4.1.4 [EBR 20]** — "All electrical and electronic equipment shall be bonded using the methods described in section 5.1 to provide a low impedance path from the equipment enclosure to structure."
- **4.1.4b [EBR 21]** — "All Class R bond paths to structure, and the joints in that path, shall be designed such that the inductance and overall impedance, including resonances, are low enough to prevent interference at the frequencies of interest."
- **4.1.4b(1) [EBR 22]** — "The direct current (dc) resistance across each joint in the path shall not exceed 2.5 milliohms."
- **4.1.4c [EBR 23]** (Change 1) — "The design and construction of the outer mold line of the vehicle shall implement Class R electrical bonding between all outer mold line components so as to inherently provide a uniform low impedance enclosure surrounding the vehicle."

Stated intent (4.1.4 opening text): "The intent of Class R bonding is to provide a uniform low impedance path for all electrical equipment at radio frequencies."

That is the whole of the Class R requirement. A designer looking for a pass/fail ohm number at a frequency will not find one, because the standard deliberately does not provide one.

## 2. The rationale text that settles the question

Appendix B.3.4 (Appendix A.3.4 in un-changed Rev A) is explicit. Quoting the standard:

> "There is no RF design basis for the historical 2.5-milliohm requirement except to ensure a good metal-to-metal contact that can be expected to be consistent. The basic requirement is to have low impedance at the frequency or frequencies of interest. The value of this impedance depends upon the quality of the surface preparation (e.g., the chemical formulation used for the conversion coating, and the thickness thereof), the area of the faying surfaces in contact, and the amount of pressure holding the surfaces together. **The impedance of an acceptable bond may be in the ohms range for RF even though the dc resistance is less than 2.5 milliohms. The resistance is overshadowed by the inductive reactance of the configuration.**"

> "The 2.5-milliohm dc resistance requirement is good for a standard, but one should not assume a good RF bond exists just because the dc resistance is less than 2.5 milliohms. Also, extra effort need not be made just to satisfy the dc requirement if the RF impedance is much higher due to the inductance of the configuration. Look at the whole configuration to get the lowest impedance possible at the frequencies of interest to produce a good RF bond."

> "The total impedance across the joint is equal to the resistance at frequencies from dc to the point where the inductive reactance approaches the resistance. The impedance due to inductance then increases at 20 dB per decade of frequency to a frequency where the inductive reactance and the capacitive reactance are equal. At this parallel resonant frequency, the impedance may rise to thousands of ohms depending on the ratio of reactance to resistance (Q) in the circuit..."

Consequence: quoting "2.5 mΩ" as *the* Class R RF impedance limit is a category error — it is a DC figure, the standard says so, and the standard says a compliant joint can be tens of ohms at RF. Equally, inventing an ohm/frequency pair (e.g. "0.1 Ω at 1 MHz") is not traceable to NASA-STD-4003A.

## 3. Every number the standard does attach to a Class R bond

| Quantity | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| DC resistance across each joint in the Class R path | **≤ 2.5 mΩ** | 4.1.4b(1) [EBR 22] |
| DC resistance of each joint in the backshell-to-case path | **≤ 2.5 mΩ** | 4.1.4.1 (connectors / shield termination) |
| DC resistance of each shield termination | **≤ 2.5 mΩ** | 4.1.4.1 shield-termination text (Change 1) |
| DC resistance of antenna return path to structure | **≤ 2.5 mΩ** | Appendix antenna guidance (Rev A / Change 1) |
| Bond strap length-to-width ratio, where a strap is unavoidable | **≤ 5:1**, strap flat in cross-section | Appendix B.3.4 / design guidance |
| RF impedance limit in ohms at a stated frequency | **none specified** | 4.1.4b [EBR 21] is performance-based |

The summary table in the standard states the same thing in tabular form: Class R — "Bonding resistance requirement, 2.5 milliohms or less. Low inductance required"; and "Requires low RF impedance at high frequency. Direct contact preferred. No jumpers. Short, wide strap may be used as last resort."

## 4. Why the standard is written this way — and what a designer must do instead

Inductive reactance dominates any real bond above a few tens of kilohertz. A 100 mm × 20 mm × 0.5 mm copper strap (already at the 5:1 limit) has a free-space self-inductance of roughly 56 nH:

X = 2πfL, with L ≈ 56.5 nH

| Frequency | Reactance X | Comment |
|---|---|---|
| 10 kHz | 3.6 mΩ | already above the 2.5 mΩ dc limit |
| 100 kHz | 35 mΩ | 14× the dc limit |
| 1 MHz | 0.36 Ω | sub-ohm, not milliohm |
| 10 MHz | 3.6 Ω | "ohms range," as Appendix B.3.4 says |
| 100 MHz | 36 Ω (before self-resonance) | behaviour is resonance-dominated; the standard warns impedance "may rise to thousands of ohms" at parallel resonance |

A DC milliohm measurement therefore tells you almost nothing about RF performance, which is exactly why the standard refuses to state an RF ohm limit: the acceptable value depends on the noise current, the frequency band, and the emissions/susceptibility budget of the specific vehicle. The standard says so: the basic requirement is "low impedance at the frequency or frequencies of interest."

**Procedure a designer should follow (this part is engineering practice, not a quotation):**

1. **List the frequencies of interest** for the joint: transmitter fundamental and harmonics, receiver bands, switching-converter harmonics, ESD/lightning spectral content, and any structural resonance (a bond whose length approaches a quarter wavelength can re-radiate; the standard warns of this explicitly for Class R straps).
2. **Establish the noise current** I_noise that will flow through the bond at each frequency (cable shield common-mode current, chassis-to-structure current, filter return current). Use measured data where available; otherwise bound it.
3. **Establish the allowable voltage** V_allow across the bond at that frequency, from the EMI/EMC budget: the radiated-emissions limit, the receiver sensitivity, or the shield-effectiveness target.
4. **Compute the derived limit:** Z_limit(f) = V_allow(f) / I_noise(f).
   - Example A: 5 mA of shield common-mode current, 5 mV of allowable developed voltage → Z_limit = 5 mV / 5 mA = **1.0 Ω**.
   - Example B: 20 mA of current, 2 mV allowable → Z_limit = 2 mV / 20 mA = **100 mΩ**.
   These are program-derived limits; NASA-STD-4003A neither supplies nor endorses a particular value. Record the derivation in the EMI control plan / bonding control document.
5. **Design to beat the derived limit with margin** using the standard's own design preferences: direct metal-to-metal contact over a large faying area (preferred; no jumpers), flat wide strap only as a last resort with length:width ≤ 5:1, shortest possible path, no reliance on fastener threads as the primary bonding path, and awareness that a low-Q joint can resonate.
6. **Verify both criteria**: DC resistance ≤ 2.5 mΩ per joint *and* the derived RF impedance limit at the frequencies of interest.

## 5. Verification and measurement practice

- **DC resistance:** four-wire (Kelvin) milliohm measurement of the assembled joint, meter resolution ≤ 0.1 mΩ, joint in its flight configuration (bonding through the actual fastener/plating stack, not a coupon substitute unless verified by similarity). Acceptance: ≤ 2.5 mΩ per joint, per 4.1.4b(1).
- **Low inductance / RF impedance:** the standard's historical text states that Class R and Class L bonds "require low inductance paths as well as low resistance. The low inductance path shall be verified by analysis and inspection," and that "Class R bonds should be low impedance at the frequency of interest. Calculations should be made to determine the impedance of any RF bond other than direct metal-to-metal contact over a large surface area." So a calculation of strap/joint inductance and the resulting X(f) curve, plus inspection of the physical configuration (faying area, surface finish, pressure, strap geometry), is an acceptable and standard-sanctioned verification path. Where a measured number is required by the program, use a vector impedance analyzer / network analyzer with a suitable fixture at the frequencies of interest, and be alert to fixture inductance and resonance artifacts.
- **Sampling:** testing every joint is not required. Process qualification plus verification by similarity is the standard's stated approach; the procuring agency may require test of specific joints (e.g. all antenna installations, all electronic equipment).

## 6. Things that are commonly confused with the Class R requirement

- **2.5 mΩ is not an RF specification.** It is a DC contact-quality check. See Section 2 above.
- **Class R is not a substitute for Class H.** Class H (shock/fire hazard, 0.1 Ω or less, high current) carries fault current — tens of amperes — whereas Class R carries noise currents of milliamperes. A Class R bond cannot be credited for fault-current return, and a Class H bond is not automatically a good RF bond.
- **Class R is not Class S.** Class S (electrostatic charge, ~1 Ω) is a separate requirement, e.g. for fluid-carrying tubing and external surfaces.
- **Where a bond serves multiple purposes**, the strictest applicable class governs (the standard's own example: an avionics unit needs Class R for RF and Class H for fault current, so the bond must be low-inductance with ≤ 2.5 mΩ dc *and* carry the maximum fault current).

## 7. Revision, tailoring, and citation caveats

- The EBR numbers ([EBR 20]–[EBR 23]) and the appendix designation **B.3.4** apply to **NASA-STD-4003A with Change 1** (revalidated 13 March 2026 per the published file). Un-changed **Rev A** has the same substantive 4.1.4 a/b/b(1) text without the EBR tags and refers to **Appendix A.3.4**; Change 1 adds **4.1.4c** (outer mold line enclosure). Cite the revision you are actually under.
- A program may tailor the standard or invoke a supplemental bonding document (e.g. ISS-specific bonding requirements, or a project bonding control document) that *does* impose a numeric RF impedance at a stated frequency with a stated meter and test setup. If your program has such a tailoring, that number — not NASA-STD-4003A — is your acceptance criterion, and it should be quoted from the tailoring document, not from the standard.
- No waiver or tailoring is assumed here.

## 8. Suggested clause for a project bonding control document

> "Class R bonds shall be installed per NASA-STD-4003A w/Change 1, 4.1.4. Each joint in a Class R bond path shall exhibit a DC resistance not greater than 2.5 milliohms when measured four-wire in the assembled configuration. In addition, the impedance of each Class R bond path, including strap inductance and any resonances, shall not exceed Z_limit(f) = [program value] ohms over the band [f1–f2], where Z_limit is derived in the project EMI control plan from the allowable bond voltage and the maximum expected bond current at each frequency. Compliance shall be shown by calculation of path inductance and impedance versus frequency, by inspection of faying-surface preparation and contact area, and, where designated by the procuring agency, by measurement with an RF impedance analyzer at [frequencies]. Bond straps, where unavoidable, shall be flat in cross-section with a length-to-width ratio not exceeding 5:1, and shall be sized so that no bond element approaches a quarter wavelength at any frequency of interest."

Fill in the bracketed values from your own EMI budget — NASA-STD-4003A will not fill them in for you, by design.

blocked_on.why: Ask 1 — NASA-STD-4003A specifies no maximum RF impedance in ohms at any stated frequency for a Class R bond joint. The only numeric limit the standard attaches to a Class R joint is a DC resistance (2.5 milliohms per joint), and Appendix B.3.4 explicitly disclaims any RF design basis for that number and states that an acceptable RF bond impedance 'may be in the ohms range.' Any ohm/frequency figure supplied for this ask would be invented rather than read from the standard.

results.value: Performance-based, not numeric: 4.1.4b [EBR 21] requires the Class R bond path and every joint in it to be designed so inductance and overall impedance, including resonances, are low enough to prevent interference at the frequencies of interest; 4.1.4b(1) [EBR 22] adds dc resistance <= 2.5 milliohms across each joint; 4.1.4a [EBR 20] requires bonding per section 5.1 methods (direct metal-to-metal contact preferred, no jumpers, short wide flat strap only as last resort); 4.1.4c [EBR 23] requires Class R bonding across all outer mold line components

Hardware Engineering Gotchas
Real-world hardware caveats, PCB layout constraints and silicon errata to know before manufacturing.
Critical
Combined Package and Port Group Current Limits
The 40 mA per-pin absolute maximum is a stress limit, not a guaranteed drive capability (output voltage is characterized at 20 mA and VCC = 5 V under the stated temperature conditions); total current through all VCC and GND pins must not exceed 200 mA. Additionally, Microchip enforces strict port group current limits: total steady-state sink current (IOL) must not exceed 100 mA each for (1) Ports C0-C5 + ADC6/ADC7, (2) Ports B0-B5 + D5-D7 + XTAL1/XTAL2, and (3) Ports D0-D4 + RESET. Total source current (IOH) must not exceed 150 mA each for (1) Ports C0-C5 + D0-D4 + ADC7 + RESET, and (2) Ports B0-B5 + D5-D7 + ADC6 + XTAL1/XTAL2.
